stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.perm.se.justification: The target states `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (i j : Fin n), (σ * Equiv.swap i j).setQ i j = σ.setR i j`, exactly matching “The set Q for σ · t_{i,j} equals the set R for σ.” The multiplication convention also agrees: the informal definition says `αβ` sends `x` to `α(β(x))`, so `σ * Equiv.swap i j` is σ after the transposition. The project bodies match the informal set definitions: `setQ` requires `i < k ∧ k < j ∧ σ j < σ k ∧ σ k < σ i`, while `setR` requires `i < k ∧ k < j ∧ σ i < σ k ∧ σ k < σ j`. Although the informal definition introduces `t_{i,j}` for distinct `i,j`, the Lean theorem quantifies over all `i j`; this is a strictly more general statement, not a weakening. Likewise, the theorem is unconditional rather than assuming `σ(i) < σ(j)`, so the parenthetical use case in the prose does not introduce a missing hypothesis.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.perm.si.justification: The blueprint says, “Every simple transposition $s_i$ is a cycle (specifically, a $2$-cycle),” with $i\in[n-1]$. The Lean signature quantifies over exactly the zero-based counterpart, `∀ {n : ℕ} (i : Fin (n - 1))`, and `simpleTransposition i` has body `Equiv.swap ⟨↑i, …⟩ ⟨↑i + 1, …⟩`. Thus it swaps two distinct adjacent elements and fixes all others, so it is specifically a 2-cycle. The shift from textbook `[n] = {1,…,n}` to `Fin n = {0,…,n-1}` merely relabels the same `n-1` adjacent transpositions; the universal claim is unchanged. For `n ≤ 1`, `Fin (n - 1)` is empty, matching the absence of simple transpositions.

The blueprint states: “Every simple transposition $s_i$ is a swap (i.e., a $2$-cycle).” The Lean theorem quantifies over exactly the available simple-transposition indices, `∀ {n : ℕ} (i : Fin (n - 1))`, and concludes `Equiv.Perm.IsSwap (AlgebraicCombinatorics.simpleTransposition i)`. By the dependency body, `simpleTransposition i` is `Equiv.swap ⟨↑i, …⟩ ⟨↑i + 1, …⟩`, while `Equiv.Perm.IsSwap` means that the permutation is a transposition. The use of `Fin n = {0,…,n-1}` and indices `Fin (n-1)` is precisely the stated Lean indexing convention; for `n < 2` the index type is empty, matching the absence of simple transpositions. Thus the formal and informal statements agree.

The blueprint says: “For $n \ge 2$ and $i \in [n-1]$, we have $s_i \ne \operatorname{id}$.” The Lean signature states `∀ {n : ℕ} (i : Fin (n - 1)), simpleTransposition i ≠ 1`. Here `Fin (n - 1)` is the zero-based representation of the `n-1` valid simple-transposition indices, and the dependency defines `simpleTransposition i` as the swap of `i` and `i+1` in `Fin n`; `1` is the identity permutation. Although Lean does not explicitly bind `n ≥ 2`, an inhabitant `i : Fin (n - 1)` can exist only when `n - 1 > 0`, hence only when `n ≥ 2`. For `n < 2` the universal statement is vacuous. The shift from textbook `[n] = {1,…,n}` to Lean’s `Fin n = {0,…,n-1}` is the documented representation change, not a mathematical restriction.

The informal claim has two parts: “The support of $s_i$ is exactly $\{i,i+1\}$, and has cardinality $2$.” These are formalized respectively by `Equiv.Perm.support (AlgebraicCombinatorics.simpleTransposition i) = {⟨↑i, ⋯⟩, ⟨↑i + 1, ⋯⟩}` and `(Equiv.Perm.support (AlgebraicCombinatorics.simpleTransposition i)).card = 2`. The dependency defines `simpleTransposition i` as `Equiv.swap ⟨↑i, ⋯⟩ ⟨↑i + 1, ⋯⟩`, exactly the permutation exchanging those two points, while `Equiv.Perm.support` is the finset of nonfixed points. The binder `∀ {n : ℕ} (i : Fin (n - 1))` faithfully encodes the informal `n ∈ ℕ` and `i ∈ [n-1]` under the project’s documented zero-based representation of `[n]` by `Fin n`; for `n ≤ 1` both index sets are empty. Thus the two Lean theorems together express exactly the blueprint statement.

The target quantifies exactly over the intended data: `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (i : Fin n)`, matching “For each i ∈ [n]” with permutations represented on `Fin n` under the stated zero-based convention. Its conclusion `↑(σ i) = σ.smallerBefore i + σ.lehmerEntry i` matches `σ(i) = s(σ,i) + ℓ_i(σ)`. The dependency bodies give precisely the informal definitions: `smallerBefore` is `{j | j < i ∧ σ j < σ i}.card`, and `lehmerEntry` is `{j | i < j ∧ σ i > σ j}.card`. Thus the right side partitions the values below `σ(i)` according to whether their positions occur before or after `i`; in the `Fin n = {0,…,n−1}` convention their total is the natural value `↑(σ i)`. No additional hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers are present.

The formal binders `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (hn : n > 0)` exactly encode “For σ ∈ S_n with n > 0” under the stated `Fin n = {0, …, n-1}` convention. The conclusion `↑(σ ⟨0, hn⟩) = σ.lehmerEntry ⟨0, hn⟩` is precisely `σ(0) = ℓ₀(σ)`: the coercion `↑` takes the value of `σ(0) : Fin n` to its natural-number value, while `lehmerEntry` is defined as `{j | i < j ∧ σ i > σ j}.card`, matching the informal Lehmer-entry definition. The hypothesis `hn` is not added drift; it is explicitly required informally and supplies the proof that `0 : Fin n` exists.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.perm.sm.justification: The indexing conventions disagree. The blueprint fixes `[n]` as `\{1,2,\ldots,n\}` and states `s(σ,i) + g(σ,i) = i`. Thus an element labelled `i` has only `i-1` elements `j<i`; indeed the accompanying partition argument yields `i-1`, not `i`. The formal declaration instead binds `(i : Fin n)`, where `Fin.val i` ranges from `0` to `n-1`, and concludes `σ.smallerBefore i + σ.largerBefore i = ↑i`. This correctly counts the `i.val` preceding zero-based indices, but under the natural correspondence with the blueprint's one-based label, `↑i` represents informal `i-1`. The difference enters through the target binder `(i : Fin n)` together with the RHS coercion `↑i`, relative to the informal definition of `[n]`. To literally formalize the stated one-based equation using `Fin n`, the RHS would have to be `↑i + 1` after translating labels, though that proposition conflicts with the blueprint's own counting definitions and is false. Alternatively, changing the blueprint convention to `[n]={0,…,n-1}` (or changing its RHS to `i-1`) would make the present theorem faithful.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.perm.su.justification: The Lean target states `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)), ∑ i, σ.lehmerEntry i = σ.length`, where `Equiv.Perm.length` is definitionally `σ.inversions.card` and `σ.inversions` consists of pairs satisfying `p.1 < p.2 ∧ σ p.2 < σ p.1`. Its `lehmerEntry` correctly matches the informal definition of `ℓ_i(σ)` as the number of `j` with `i < j` and `σ(i) > σ(j)`. However, the informal statement’s right-hand side is merely called “the length,” `ℓ(σ)`, and the package supplies no informal definition saying that this length is the number of inversions. Thus the package does not determine whether the project definition `Equiv.Perm.length := σ.inversions.card` has the intended blueprint meaning. An informal definition of `ℓ(σ)` is needed; if it defines length as the inversion count, the declaration is faithful.

The blueprint states: “For n ≥ 2, ∑_{σ ∈ S_n} (-1)^σ = 0.” The formal theorem quantifies over every finite nontrivial type, `∀ {α : Type u_1} [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α] [Nontrivial α], ∑ σ, ↑(Equiv.Perm.sign σ) = 0`. Here `Equiv.Perm α` is the symmetric group of the finite set α, and `[Nontrivial α]` says α has at least two elements, corresponding to `n ≥ 2`. `Equiv.Perm.sign` returns `1` for even permutations and `-1` for odd ones, matching the informal `(-1)^σ`; coercion gives its integer value. Quantifying over arbitrary finite nontrivial types is a coordinate-free, strictly more general version of quantifying over `[n]`, which is permitted. `[DecidableEq α]` supplies computational structure needed for the finite permutation/sign constructions and is not a substantive mathematical restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.perm.ti.justification: The target states `∀ {X : Type u_1} [DecidableEq X] (i j : X), (transposition i j)⁻¹ = transposition i j`, exactly asserting that a transposition is its own inverse. The dependency defines `transposition i j` as `Equiv.swap i j`, matching the informal definition of the permutation exchanging `i` and `j`. Although the blueprint introduces it for “two distinct elements,” the Lean theorem quantifies over all `i j : X`; this is strictly more general, since it also covers `i = j`, where the swap is the identity. The `[DecidableEq X]` binder is an encoding requirement used to define `Equiv.swap`, rather than an additional mathematical hypothesis affecting the involutivity claim.

The target states `∀ {X : Type u_1} [DecidableEq X] (i j : X), transposition i j * transposition i j = 1`. By the dependency body, `transposition i j` is exactly `Equiv.swap i j`, matching the informal transposition, and multiplication and `1` on `Equiv.Perm X` represent composition and the identity as fixed by the informal definitions. Although `def.perm.tij` introduces transpositions for distinct `i` and `j`, the Lean theorem quantifies over all `i j`, so it is strictly more general and in particular implies the distinct case. The `[DecidableEq X]` binder is an encoding requirement needed by `Equiv.swap`, not an additional mathematical condition on the claimed involution property.

The blueprint states: “For any two distinct elements $i,j$ of a set $X$, we have $t_{i,j}=t_{j,i}$.” The Lean target proves `∀ {X : Type u_1} [DecidableEq X] (i j : X), transposition i j = transposition j i`, with no distinctness hypothesis, so it is strictly more general in `i,j` and in particular implies the stated distinct case. The dependency defines `transposition i j` as `Equiv.swap i j`, matching the informal transposition. The `[DecidableEq X]` binder is the computational instance required by `Equiv.swap` and thus encodes the formal setting rather than adding a mathematical restriction to the symmetry claim.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.permsma.justification: The blueprint states: “If $|P| \ne |Q|$, then $\operatorname{Perm}(P,Q)=\varnothing$.” The target quantifies over arbitrary `P Q : Finset (Fin n)` and assumes exactly `P.card ≠ Q.card`, then concludes `AlgebraicCombinatorics.CauchyBinet.permsMapping P Q = ∅`. By definition, `permsMapping P Q` is `{σ | imageFinset σ P = Q}`, matching the informal definition $\operatorname{Perm}(P,Q)=\{\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(P)=Q\}$. Moreover, `imageFinset σ P` is `Finset.map` under the bijection `σ`, matching the stated image $\{\sigma(i)\mid i\in P\}$. The use of `Fin n` in place of $[n]$ is explicitly authorized by the informal convention, and there are no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.car.justification: The blueprint says: “The number of derangements of $[n]$ … agrees with Mathlib’s derangement count.” The target states for every natural number, `∀ (n : ℕ), Fintype.card (Derangement (Fin n)) = numDerangements n`. Here `Fin n` is the canonical type of natural numbers below `n`, hence the formal realization of `[n]`; `Fintype.card` gives the number of elements; and `numDerangements n` is documented as “The number of derangements of an `n`-element set.” Moreover, the dependency defines `Derangement α` as `{ σ // ∀ (x : α), σ x ≠ x }`, with `σ` a permutation, exactly matching the informal definition “a permutation of $X$ that has no fixed points.” The only required `DecidableEq` and `Fintype` instances are automatically available for `Fin n` and merely encode finitary cardinality computation; they add no mathematical restriction.

The formal binders `∀ (m n : ℕ) (I : Finset (Fin n))` match “Let m, n ∈ ℕ and let I be a subset of [n],” using the stipulated replacement of `[n]` by `Fin n`. The subtype `{ f // ∀ i ∈ I, i ∉ Set.range f }` consists exactly of functions `f : Fin m → Fin n` whose image omits every `i ∈ I`, and `Fintype.card` counts those functions. The equality to `(n - I.card) ^ m` is precisely the claimed `(n - |I|)^m`. No additional mathematically substantive hypotheses or restricted quantifiers are present.

The formal binders `∀ (m n : ℕ) (t : Finset (Fin n))` represent arbitrary finite subsets `t ⊆ [n]`. The dependency defines `S_avoid m n i` as `{f | i ∉ Set.range f}`, exactly matching `S_avoid(i) = { f : [m] → [n] | i ∉ im f }`. By `Finset.inf`, `(t.inf (S_avoid m n))` is the finite intersection over `i ∈ t` (with the empty intersection interpreted as the universal finite set), and `.card = (n - t.card) ^ m` is precisely the claimed cardinality `(n - |t|)^m`. No additional hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers are present.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.der.justification: The binder `∀ {α : Type u_1} [IsEmpty α]` exactly formalizes an arbitrary empty type. The conclusion `∃ d, ↑d = 1`, together with `Derangement α := { σ // ∀ (x : α), σ x ≠ x }`, asserts that there is a derangement whose underlying permutation is `1`, i.e. the identity permutation. This matches “The identity permutation is a derangement of the empty type (vacuously, it has no fixed points).” Moreover, on an empty type every self-permutation is the identity, so the derangement type has exactly this one element, yielding the stated consequence “Hence D₀ = 1.” Quantifying over every type carrying `[IsEmpty α]` is a harmless generalization of choosing a particular empty set.

The binder `∀ {α : Type u_1} [Nonempty α] (d : ...Derangement α)` exactly covers every derangement of every nonempty type. By the dependency body, such a `d` is a permutation satisfying `∀ x, d x ≠ x`. The conclusion `↑d ≠ 1` says its underlying permutation is not `1`, which for `Equiv.Perm α` is the identity permutation. Thus it matches “If α is nonempty, then no derangement of α equals the identity permutation.” For a singleton type every permutation is the identity, so this also yields the stated special case `D₁ = 0`.

The informal statement asserts both “D₂ = 1” and “D₃ = 2.” The two target declarations state exactly `numDerangements 2 = 1` and `numDerangements 3 = 2`. The base-library definition fixes `numDerangements : ℕ → ℕ` as “the number of derangements of an `n`-element set,” matching the informal definition of a derangement as a permutation with no fixed points. There are no additional binders or hypotheses, and together the two declarations faithfully formalize the conjunction of the two claimed small counts.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.equ.justification: The target gives, for every type `α`, an equivalence `AlgebraicCombinatorics.InclusionExclusion.Derangement α ≃ ↑(derangements α)`. By the project definition, the left side is `{ σ // ∀ (x : α), σ x ≠ x }`, namely permutations of `α` with no fixed points. By the base-library docstring, `derangements α` is the set of permutations with no fixed points, and `↑(derangements α)` is its subtype of elements. Since `α ≃ β` is a function with a two-sided inverse, this is exactly the claimed bijection between the derangements defined in Definition `def.pie.dera` and Mathlib’s fixed-point-free permutations. There are no added hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.fac.justification: The target quantifies only over naturals: `∀ (m n : ℕ), ...`, and the project dependency likewise fixes `numSurj : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ`. By contrast, the blueprint defines `[n]` for `n ∈ ℤ`, explicitly including nonpositive indices, and defines `numSurj(m,n)` using `[m]` and `[n]`. Although `n!` naturally restricts the meaningful claim to nonnegative `n`, nothing similarly restricts `m`; negative `m` denotes the empty set under the supplied definition. Thus the Lean binder `m : ℕ` narrows the blueprint's index range. To be faithful, the dependency should accept the blueprint’s integer indices (interpreting `[k]` as empty for `k ≤ 0`), and the theorem should quantify over integer `m` and nonnegative `n` (or an equivalent encoding).

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.moe.justification: The conclusion matches the displayed formula: Lean states `∀ I ⊆ S, a I = ∑ J ∈ I.powerset, (-1) ^ (I \ J).card • b J`, where `I.powerset` ranges over `J ⊆ I` and `•` is the integer scalar action. The `DecidableEq α` binder is an encoding requirement for finset difference. However, the blueprint says only “under the same hypotheses,” referring to Theorem `thm.pie.moeb`, while that theorem and its hypotheses are absent from the package. Consequently, it is impossible to determine whether Lean’s antecedent `(∀ I ⊆ S, b I = ∑ J ∈ I.powerset, a J)` and its ambient binders `{S}`, `[AddCommGroup A]`, and `[Module ℤ A]` are exactly those intended. The package would need the statement of `thm.pie.moeb` (or an explicit informal proof-dependency giving its hypotheses) to decide faithfulness.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.rul.justification: The binders `∀ {α : Type u_1} [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α] (n : ℕ) (satisfiesRule : Fin n → Finset α)` faithfully encode a finite type `α`, `n` rules, and subsets `A_i`; `Fin n` is exactly the index range `{0, …, n−1}`. The left side `↑{u | ∀ (i : Fin n), u ∉ satisfiesRule i}.card` counts elements violating every rule. The right side ranges over `I ∈ Finset.univ.powerset`, hence all subsets of the rule indices, and sums `(-1) ^ I.card * ↑{u | ∀ i ∈ I, u ∈ satisfiesRule i}.card`, exactly matching the stated alternating sum. The casts place cardinalities in `ℤ`, as required for signs. `[Fintype α]` is required by the blueprint’s “finite type,” while `[DecidableEq α]` is an encoding requirement for `Finset` membership/filtering rather than an additional mathematical restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.siz.justification: The target quantifies over a finite ambient type and finite family data via `[Fintype U]`, `s : Finset ι`, and `A : ι → Finset U`, matching “for a finite type U, finite index set s, and subsets A_i of U.” Its equation `↑(s.inf fun i => (A i)ᶜ).card = ∑ I ∈ s.powerset, (-1) ^ I.card * ↑(I.inf A).card` is exactly the integer-valued identity `|⋂_{i∈s} A_i^c| = ∑_{I∈s.powerset} (-1)^{|I|}|⋂_{i∈I}A_i|`. By `Finset.inf`, the two infima are the indicated finite intersections, including the usual top/universal-set interpretation for an empty intersection. The binders `[DecidableEq ι]` and `[DecidableEq U]` provide the decidability needed for finset operations and complements; they are formal encoding requirements rather than mathematically substantive restrictions on the finite sets in the blueprint.

The blueprint assumes “Let α be a finite type and A₀,…,Aₙ₋₁ be n subsets of α,” matched by `∀ {α : Type u_1} [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α] (n : ℕ) (A : Fin n → Finset α)`. Here `Fin n` is exactly the index set `{0,…,n-1}`, and finsets represent subsets of the finite universe `α`. The `DecidableEq α` binder is computational structure needed for finsets and is not a mathematically contentful restriction. On the left, `Finset.univ.inf fun i => (A i)ᶜ` is the intersection over all `i : Fin n` of the complements of `A i`, hence the set of `u` outside every `Aᵢ`; its card is cast to `ℤ`. On the right, `I ∈ Finset.univ.powerset` ranges over every subset `I ⊆ Fin n`, `(-1) ^ I.card` is the required sign, and `(I.inf A).card` is the cardinality of `⋂ i ∈ I, Aᵢ`, with the empty infimum equal to the universal finset. Thus the displayed equality agrees with the informal inclusion–exclusion formula, including the empty-index cases.

The target exactly states the complement-of-union identity: `↑(s.biUnion A)ᶜ.card` is the integer cardinality of the complement of the union over `s`, while `∑ I ∈ s.powerset, (-1) ^ I.card * ↑(I.inf A).card` sums `(-1)^{|I|}` times the cardinality of the intersection over every subset `I ⊆ s`. In particular, `Finset.inf` uses the top element for the empty intersection, as required by PIE. The binders `[Fintype α]` and `[DecidableEq α]` provide the finite ambient universe and computational finite-set structure needed for a finite complement and its cardinality; they encode the setting implicit in this size formulation. The target is actually more general than the blueprint’s indexing by `[n]`: it allows any finite index set supplied as `(s : Finset ι)`. Taking `ι = Fin n` and `s` to be the whole index set recovers the stated formulation.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.sta.justification: The target quantifies over arbitrary naturals and a surjective function via `∀ {m n : ℕ} (f : { f // Function.Surjective f })`, matching “Let `f : [m] → [n]` be surjective,” with `Fin m` and `Fin n` supplied by the stated Lean convention. The conclusion `MulAction.stabilizer (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) f = ⊥` says exactly that its stabilizer in the symmetric group is the trivial subgroup, since `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` represents `S_n` and `Subgroup.instBot` defines `⊥` as `{1}`. Finally, `permActionOnSurj` defines the action by `smul := fun σ f => ⟨σ • ↑f, …⟩`; together with the pointwise function action and the tautological permutation action, this is post-composition by `σ`, as required. The fixed commutative ring context is irrelevant to this statement, so its absence does not narrow or alter the claim.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.sum.justification: The formal binders match the blueprint: `{Q : Finset α}` represents the finite set Q, `[AddCommGroup A]` matches “A an additive abelian group,” and `f : Finset α → Finset α → A` is a harmlessly more general version of a function on pairs of subsets of Q, since every occurrence is evaluated only on `J ⊆ Q` and `P ⊆ J`. The equality `∑ J ∈ Q.powerset, ∑ P ∈ J.powerset, f J P = ∑ P ∈ Q.powerset, ∑ J ∈ Q.powerset with P ⊆ J, f J P` exactly expresses the two orders of summation in the blueprint. The binder `[DecidableEq α]` is an encoding requirement for finite-set powersets and decidable subset filtering, not a mathematically contentful restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.sur.justification: The blueprint quantifies over “a permutation of [n]” and a surjective map “f : [m] → [n]”; the elaborated binders match this as `σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)`, `f : Fin m → Fin n`, and `Function.Surjective f`. By `Function.hasSMul` together with `Equiv.Perm.applyMulAction`, `(σ • f)` is the pointwise action `x ↦ σ (f x)`, exactly the stated post-composition `σ ∘ f`. The conclusion `Function.Surjective (σ • f)` therefore precisely says that this post-composition is surjective. The replacement of `[n]` and `[m]` by `Fin n` and `Fin m` is explicitly prescribed by the informal definition.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pol.eva.justification: The blueprint quantifies over “any K-algebra,” and `def.alg.Kalg` explicitly allows `A` to be a “(noncommutative) ring.” The elaborated target instead requires `{A : Type u_2} [inst_1 : CommRing A] [inst_2 : Algebra K A]`, restricting the result to commutative algebras. This mathematically contentful added hypothesis enters through the dependency `FPS.polyEval`, whose type likewise contains `[CommRing A]`, even though its body `(Polynomial.aeval a) f` only fundamentally uses the algebra/semiring structure. The displayed equality itself correctly expands evaluation as `f.sum fun n c => (algebraMap K A) c * a ^ n`; `Polynomial.sum` is the finite sum over the polynomial’s supported coefficients. To make the declaration faithful, generalize the `A` binder in `FPS.polyEval` and `FPS.eval_def` from `[CommRing A]` to a possibly noncommutative ring structure (together with `[Algebra K A]`), as required by the blueprint’s definition of a K-algebra.

The blueprint says: “Let A be any K-algebra,” and its definition explicitly allows A to be a “(noncommutative) ring.” The elaborated target instead assumes `[inst_1 : CommRing A]`, restricting A to commutative rings. This is a mathematically contentful added hypothesis, so the Lean theorem is weaker than the blueprint statement. The restriction also enters through `FPS.polyEval`, whose signature requires `[CommRing A]`, even though its body `(Polynomial.aeval a) f` only fundamentally uses the algebra/semiring structure. To make the formalization faithful to the stated setting, replace the `CommRing A` binder in both `FPS.polyEval` and `FPS.eval_eq_finsum` with `Ring A` (together with `[Algebra K A]`). The displayed equality itself correctly represents `f[a] = ∑ n ∈ supp(f), f_n · a^n`, with scalar multiplication expressed as `(algebraMap K A) (f.coeff n) * a ^ n`.

The blueprint quantifies over “any $K$-algebra $A$,” and its definition explicitly says that $A$ is a “(noncommutative) ring.” The target instead has the binder `{A : Type u_2} [inst_1 : CommRing A] [inst_2 : Algebra K A]`, restricting $A$ to commutative rings. This is a mathematically substantive added hypothesis, so the theorem does not cover all blueprint $K$-algebras. The restriction also enters through `FPS.polyEval`, whose signature requires `[CommRing A]`, even though its body is `Polynomial.aeval a f`, whose supplied signature only requires `[Semiring A]`. To make the formalization faithful, generalize `FPS.polyEval` to accept a noncommutative ring codomain (e.g. `[Ring A] [Algebra K A]`) and likewise replace the target’s `[CommRing A]` binder by `[Ring A]`. The equality itself correctly identifies evaluation at `1` with `algebraMap K A` applied to `f.sum fun x c => c`, i.e. the finite sum of all coefficients coerced into `A`.

The blueprint quantifies over “any $K$-algebra,” and its definition explicitly says that $A$ is a “(noncommutative) ring.” The elaborated target instead requires `{A : Type u_2} [inst_1 : CommRing A] [inst_2 : Algebra K A]`, restricting the result to commutative algebras. This mathematically substantive added hypothesis makes the Lean theorem weaker. The restriction also enters through `FPS.polyEval`, whose type likewise requires `[CommRing A]`, even though its body is `Polynomial.aeval a f` and the supplied signature of `Polynomial.aeval` only requires a semiring target. To make the formalization faithful, generalize the `A` binder in both `FPS.polyEval` and `FPS.eval_eq_sum_range` from `[CommRing A]` to a noncommutative ring structure (e.g. `[Ring A]`) together with `[Algebra K A]`. The finite range itself correctly represents indices `0 ≤ n ≤ natDegree f`, since `Finset.range (f.natDegree + 1)` contains exactly those natural numbers.

The blueprint says, “For any polynomial $f\in K[x]$, we have $f[x]=f$,” with $K$ fixed as a commutative ring. The formal binders match this exactly: `∀ {K : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing K] (f : Polynomial K), ...`. Its conclusion is `FPS.polyEval f Polynomial.X = f`, and `FPS.polyEval` is defined as `(Polynomial.aeval a) f`, i.e. polynomial evaluation in a `K`-algebra. Here the equality with `f : Polynomial K` fixes the target algebra as `Polynomial K`, while `Polynomial.X` is its indeterminate. Thus the conclusion states that evaluating `f` at the indeterminate in `K[X]` returns `f`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.sf.basi.justification: The five identities involving `e 0`, `h 0`, `e 1`, `h 1`, and `p 1` match the corresponding blueprint clauses. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.sf.bk-c.justification: The target concludes column-strictness for `AlgebraicCombinatorics.benderKnuth k hk T hT`, but that dependency does not implement the blueprint’s stated parenthesis matching. T j i => Nat.card { c // T ⟨↑c, ⋯⟩ = i }`, but the package does not expose the inferred type/domain of `c`.
